title: Charlie Shavers, whose aunt he dated, and the fatherly advice
summary: Autrey dated Charlie Shavers's aunt before knowing the boy was a trumpeter, was stunned to hear him on radio, and later warned him off drugs and traded choruses with him at the Stuyvesant Casino.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: well -- I don't know. I knew Charlie from a kid, and I felt like a father to him, because I used to go around with Charlie's aunt, you know? And that's another story. I must tell you.
(Laughs.) Okay.

Because I met her, and I was playing, and he said well meet Herman Autrey, the trumpet player, don't you -- and she says oh, my nephew plays trumpet. I said yes? I said well tell him to keep studying there. Never can tell. One of these days he might get to be somebody. You know.
(Laughter.)
Doggone. I say what's his name. She say Charlie. I said well nice, Charlie Shavers. I never heard him. In fact, he wasn't around New York then. He was in school.
(Laughter.)
In Boys' Town.
(Laughter.)

So we went out balling, having a ball, running here, so one day I happened to be in the house doing something, and I turned on my radio, and beeeee! biddle diddle diddle diddle bah diddle diddle, rah! diddle diddle diddle, I said damn, that's nice! And I heard quite a bit. I said -- asked somebody, I said who's that? Who's that guy? That's Shavers. I say Who? Shavers.
(Laughter.)
I say Charlie Shavers?! He say yeah. Oh, God!
(Laughter.)

I said that's Charlie Shavers? Shoot, and when I saw him, I said man, I felt like about two cents, you know. That's this guy. Playing all that trumpet! And he could blow, I mean. I didn't usually give a damn about nobody.

So I -- but I hadn't had a chance to meet him, yet. So I -- when I did meet him, I told him the story, so he laughed, and I sat down to give him a fatherly talk. I said now take it easy. Don't do what you see a lot of these other guys doing. You don't need it! I said if you want a drink, take a drink. I say at least that's legal. You know. I told him. I said but this other stuff, you don't need it.

He said oh, okay, okay. Okay. So I felt good. I'd say well, I hope if have helped to start him on the right track, and don't -- and at least he'll think before he makes that other turn, if he ever wants to.
But he did pretty well, didn't he?
Hm?
He did pretty well.
Did pretty well!
(Laughter.)
Shoot, man, nobody -- could write and
blow, so -- and I told a lot of people what I told him I said, so we worked down on Second Avenue, at the -- the jazz jam session thing (snaps fingers) there? For --
: The Stuyvesant Casino?

Yes. So he'd -- I -- he came in there and my daughter was there then. My daughter was visiting me, you know, and I said look. Take it easy now, with the old man. I said after all, I said don't get there and make me look like a damn fool.
(Laughter.)
He says ah, don't worry about a thing. I say don't worry! What you mean, don't worry? I say my first -- another thing, my daughter's here. I said don't make me look too damn bad.
(Laughter.)
So, he takes four or five, I would take four or five, and we'd take -- and that kept up for half -- for the evening, you know, and we had lots of fun. But Charlie Shavers, I didn't care about nobody.
